A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised three Qwen2.5-Coder-3B builds from zero to 76-113 solved tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.

Machine Learning.title: When Can You Trust Your Synthetic Users? Diagnostics and Corrections for LLM Consumer Panels
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.13148v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate consumers, yet agreement with aggregate survey outcomes can conceal errors in the subgroup estimates that guide decisions. We develop a framework for deciding when to trust, correct, or abandon a synthetic consumer panel by distinguishing population mismatch from differences in conditional responses. The framework combines diagnostics for covariate overlap, conditional calibration, and stability across models with an augmented inverse probability weighting estimator that treats LLM predictions as auxiliary information. Correction requires a complete invitation frame, response indicators for everyone invited, and human outcomes for respondents, together with assumptions of missing at random and positivity. We evaluate the framework using simulations and controlled nonresponse experiments constructed from paired human and LLM responses in ANES and Twin-2K-500. In identified simulation regimes, point bias remains small when either the response model or the outcome model is correct, but nominal 95\% confidence intervals cover only 88--94\% in some regimes. When nonresponse depends on missing human outcomes, substantial bias persists and coverage approaches zero. Controlled masking of the paired datasets reproduces this contrast between successful point correction under imposed missing at random and failure under nonignorable nonresponse. These findings show why validation must address the intended population and task, and why the scope for correcting synthetic estimates depends on the available human data and the assumptions that identify the target.

Machine Learning.title: A Sentinel-2 benchmark dataset for deep-learning active-fire segmentation across 25 California wildfires, July 2020-August 2026
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.16199v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This article describes an open image dataset for developing and evaluating active-fire segmentation methods in satellite imagery. The dataset contains 2,148 image-mask pairs from 25 California wildfires, with acquisitions spanning July 2020 to August 2026. Each image is a 512x512-pixel, three-channel composite derived from Sentinel-2 Level-2A bands B12, B11 and B8A at 20 m spatial sampling. A fixed linear rendering is applied throughout the dataset. Corresponding masks distinguish background, SWIR-rule active fire and invalid observations. The masks were generated from shortwave-infrared brightness and near-infrared contrast, followed by constrained neighborhood growth. The release includes chip-level metadata and an incident-disjoint partition containing 18 training, three validation and four test fires. Among the image pairs, 841 contain active-fire labels; these labels occupy 0.0766% of all grid cells. A mask-blind analyst review covers 233 test chips and provides a separate assessment of the rule-generated labels at chip and connected-component levels. Reference training and evaluation code accompanies the data, including a ResNet-34 U-Net implementation with validation-based checkpoint and threshold selection. The archived images, masks, metadata and review annotations support research on rare-class segmentation, learning from algorithmic labels and transfer across fire incidents. The versioned dataset is deposited on Zenodo, with preparation and reuse software maintained in a public GitHub repository.

Machine Learning.title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.17736v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

Machine Learning.title: VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.20191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

Machine Learning.title: Forecast-Dojo: Replayable Environments for Benchmarking and Training LLM Forecasting Agents
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.28876v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Forecasting requires large language model (LLM) agents to gather evolving evidence, revise their beliefs, and make calibrated predictions over time. Yet evaluating and improving these capabilities is challenging because real-world events unfold continuously and outcomes may take months to resolve. We introduce Forecast-Dojo, a replayable environment that reconstructs resolved prediction-market events as sequences of dated forecasting steps, enabling reproducible evaluation, longitudinal analysis, and training from agent interactions. It comprises 1,568 Polymarket events split temporally into training and evaluation sets, alongside 18.8 million dated news articles. Across 12 models, research tools consistently improve forecasting performance, and greater capture of new evidence is associated with larger improvements over time. Nevertheless, all models trail historical market forecasts, while carrying a belief notebook across dates reduces research costs without consistently improving forecast quality. We supervise fine-tuned Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on collected trajectories from Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 to demonstrate the environment's training utility. The student's accuracy is improved from 34.8% to 42.8% on the evaluation set.

Machine Learning.title: A Corpus of Real Scam- and Spam-Call Conversations from an Active Voice-Agent Honeypot
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.29528v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Real conversations between fraudsters and their targets are among the most informative artifacts for studying telephone scams, yet also the scarcest: passive honeypots overwhelmingly capture automated messages and hang-ups, large-scale studies characterize call metadata rather than dialogue, and manual scam-baiting does not scale. We present a dataset of real scam-call conversations collected by an active voice-agent honeypot. Dedicated numbers are seeded into the lead-generation channels fraud operations harvest; inbound callers are answered by a low-latency conversational agent that adopts a plausible target persona and sustains the interaction while every call is recorded, transcribed, and automatically labeled. Over an initial 53-day window we captured 10,015 inbound scam and spam calls (6,601 with two or more turns): roughly 895 hours of audio and 328,869 transcribed turns from 5,665 distinct originating numbers. Under a holistic classifier the substantive calls are predominantly predatory-but-legal lead generation ("spam", about three in five), while about one in seven is an outright "scam" (949 in this snapshot). Each call carries a turn-level transcript, three-channel audio, per-turn latency telemetry, and layers of automatic labels, including a holistic scam/spam/legitimate judgment corroborated by independent human review (75% agreement on the binary decision). We describe the collection system, the record structure, and technical validation of the corpus's realism and label quality, including that the agent is recognized as non-human in only about 5% of engaged calls. We also benchmark established scam-detection methods, where detectors trained on published synthetic dialogue collapse in precision on real traffic.

Machine Learning.title: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Risk Assessment of Traffic Analysis Attacks on Cloud LLM Services
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.31877v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Cloud-based Large language model (LLM) services create a network-level traffic side channel that can expose model, prompt, and task behavior despite encryption. From packet sizes, directions, timing, and burst structure alone, a passive local observer can infer the serving model, the user's prompt category, and the task executed by a collaborative multi-agent system. Yet current evidence is fragmented across separate datasets and settings, limiting reproducibility and comparison. We present, to our knowledge, the first unified measurement study and public benchmark of encrypted LLM traffic across both user--LLM and multi-agent executions. The large-scale benchmark contains 60,000 user--LLM interactions across 10 models and 6 prompt categories, plus 2,838 multi-agent executions covering 10 task categories and two coordination topologies. Using only encrypted packet metadata, we assess the risk of traffic analysis attack by characterizing traffic signatures, identifying the features most associated with leakage, and testing robustness under prompt reformulation, decoding-temperature changes, larger candidate model sets, and partial traffic observation. Model fingerprinting achieves 97.7\% balanced accuracy, prompt-category fingerprinting reaches 76.7\% mean accuracy, and multi-agent task fingerprinting achieves up to 90.7\% accuracy. Prompt reformulation weakens but does not remove model-specific leakage, and task fingerprints remain detectable even from a single agent's traffic.

Machine Learning.title: SRHarness: A Harness for Agentic Symbolic Regression
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2609.35501v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent agentic symbolic regression approaches increasingly rely on large language models to analyze data, select scientific operations, and refine hypotheses over long search trajectories. In such systems, performance depends not only on the underlying model and search strategy, but also on the runtime infrastructure that supports scientific search. We introduce SRHarness, a domain-specific harness for agentic symbolic regression built around three mechanisms: composable scientific actions that provide a common interface over raw, transformed, and candidate-derived quantities; persistent scientific state that retains evaluated hypotheses and exposes compact model-facing views; and trajectory lifecycle management that coordinates continuation, branching, restart, and termination. On LLM-SRBench, SRHarness consistently improves both numerical generalization and symbolic recovery under matched LLM backbones. With DeepSeek-v4-flash-0731, it achieves 93.69% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform, compared with 62.16% for SR-Scientist, and retains 72.97% accuracy on an anonymized variant that removes scientific descriptions and variable semantics, versus 39.64% for SR-Scientist. Under the same DeepSeek-v4-flash-0731 backbone, SRHarness also substantially outperforms Codex (72.97% vs. 20.72%) and reaches performance comparable to Codex with GPT-5.5, while simply providing Codex with the same scientific tools does not reproduce this advantage. These results show that effective agentic symbolic regression depends not only on models or tools, but also on structured runtime support for organizing scientific actions, accumulated hypotheses, and long-horizon search.

Machine Learning.title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.02626v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

Machine Learning.title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation for Non-Monotone $k$-Submodular Maximization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.04049v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the maximization of a nonnegative $k$-submodular function, not assumed monotone, in which each of $n$ elements receives one of $k\ge2$ labels or stays unselected and the selected elements must satisfy a constraint. For a compact convex down-closed region $P\subseteq[0,1]^n$ of fractional selection vectors, the diagonal level $\zeta(P)=\max\{t\in[0,1]:t(1,\ldots,1)\in P\}$ is the largest selection probability that can be given to all elements at once; it equals $r/n$ for a uniform matroid of rank $r$, and $\zeta(P)=1$ means that the constraint is vacuous. We give approximation coefficients that increase continuously with $\zeta$. They come from one inequality for the multilinear extension of the objective: the algorithm computes an action without querying the objective, and objective feedback gives a comparator-independent update direction. For $k\ge3$, feasibility of the action reduces to three polynomial inequalities in one variable; for $k=2$ the profile is closed form. At $\zeta=0$ the coefficients are $0.4456\ldots$ for $k=2$ and $0.4541\ldots$ for every $k\ge3$. For every finite $k\ge3$ they reach $1/2$ above an explicit level, which is $0.4026\ldots$ for $k=3,4,5$, and at $\zeta=1$ they reach $1/2$ for $k=2$, $(\sqrt{17}-3)/2$ for $k=3,4$, and $k/(2k-1)$ for $k\ge5$. Online linear optimization gives $O(\sqrt T)$ approximate regret, with gradient feedback or with value queries made after each action. The coefficients carry over to matroids, with expected and high-probability guarantees, and to any fixed number of knapsacks: the zero-level coefficients hold on every instance, and the larger ones when items are small or when prefix enumeration keeps the diagonal level on one branch. For one budget the enumeration exponent is $O(1/\varepsilon)$.

Machine Learning.title: Representation-Aligned Auxiliary Supervision for Language Model Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.04098v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language models exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet adapting them to structured domains remains challenging and can yield inconsistent outcomes. We identify representation compatibility, the extent to which a model effectively processes a representation for a structured task, as a key factor in adaptation. We study this in chess, which provides a controlled testbed with precise semantics, computable optimal actions, and multiple state representations, including a symbolic encoding (FEN) and a spatial format (ASCII). We find that models often process semantically equivalent inputs substantially differently, affecting both learning and generalization. Building on this observation, we propose representation-aligned auxiliary supervision, which uses environment-derived tasks expressed in compatible representations to improve adaptation to structured domains. Across models and representations, auxiliary supervision consistently improves optimal-move prediction relative to target-only training under identical target data. Tasks that expose environment dynamics provide larger and most consistent gains than surface-level or static supervision, while remaining competitive with substantially increasing the amount of target-task data. Moreover, ASCII-trained models transfer more effectively to FEN than FEN-trained models do to ASCII, even surpassing the FEN target-only baseline on FEN evaluation. The gains also extend beyond optimal-move prediction to open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation. Overall, our results show that auxiliary supervision in model-compatible representations can enable effective adaptation in structured domains.

Machine Learning.title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.04933v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Perturbation Magnitude: Direction-Dependent Responses in Multimodal Geometric Representations
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.08533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Geometric alignment scores based on Gram determinants provide a compact way to model higher-order consistency among modalities, yet how such scores respond to modality degradation is poorly understood. This paper asks whether the response of a multimodal geometric score is determined primarily by the magnitude of the perturbation-induced displacement. Using frozen cohorts from MSR-VTT (N=878) and DiDeMo (N=980), we apply controlled video blur and audio noise and analyze the response in the relational geometry on which the score is defined. Displacement magnitude explains at most 15% of the out-of-sample variance in the absolute response, and magnitude-matched pairs respond systematically differently, so scalar magnitude does not organize the response. The closed-form first-order expansion of the Gramian volume yields the Directional Geometric Response (DGR): the projection of the displacement onto the local volume gradient, which jointly captures the clean operating point, displacement magnitude, and displacement direction. The absolute first-order DGR term explains the observed response with out-of-sample R^2 of 0.838-0.969, matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963, and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989, whereas the tested direction-free alternatives remain weak or unstable under the corresponding evaluation protocols. A pre-specified gain-normalization candidate, V/(g_V+eps), fails its predictability and clean-order gates. DGR uses the observed degraded-state displacement and is therefore an explanatory quantity, not a deployment-time predictor: geometric response depends on where the representation operates, how far degradation moves the relational geometry, and in which direction it moves.

Machine Learning.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

Machine Learning.title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.17690v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

Machine Learning.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.17718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.19781v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables language models to generate graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints, such as chemical valence and ordering rules, thereby guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences while sticking to standard language modeling for effective training. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.

Machine Learning.title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.21433v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.

Machine Learning.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.21561v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

Machine Learning.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.22454v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill makes mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, but what it damages has not been measured. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions in four MoE families on short-answer question answering. At half the experts the F1 loss is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but no longer answers briefly. The loss is made at a few tokens: the two chat-template tokens before the answer in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and the first 8-32 tokens, where the instruction sits, in DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Keeping them at full experts removes most of the F1 loss and about half and a fifth of the increase in answer NLL. These tokens are not the familiar suspects: reduction leaves the first-token sink within 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most a quarter of the loss. On real prompts the localisation becomes a placement rule: with about 4% of tokens at full experts, putting them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while the same budget scattered in the documents is about 3 points worse in both prespecified primary tests of this comparison. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts.

Machine Learning.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.22883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.

Machine Learning.title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.26833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

Machine Learning.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.27606v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

Machine Learning.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.28356v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted at BMVC 2026. Project page: this https URL

Machine Learning.title: A Reverse-Gold Theorem: Positive-Data Identification by Substrate-Bounded Contrastive Learners
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.28747v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Gold's theorem shows that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a superfinite class from positive presentations alone. We prove a positive result of a different shape. Fix an innate \emph{recursive contrast operator} $R$ mapping any string to a finite set of structurally bounded perturbations of it, and a discriminative scorer of bounded capacity trained by InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation \citep{vandenoord2018,macollins2018} on self-generated perturbations. Under a faithfulness condition relating operator, scorer, and target, the trained scorer achieves \emph{PAC conditional identification} from positive data alone: with high probability it ranks all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of positives above every out-of-language perturbation in their own orbit, with sample complexity polynomial in the capacity, the orbit size, the score bound, and $1/\varepsilon$. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. The ranking guarantee lifts to a global membership classifier under a margin condition, and the same operator composed with the learned scorer is a normalization-free Metropolis--Hastings generator. We instantiate the hypotheses for substitutable context-free languages \citep{clarkeyraud2007} and the subregular classes \citep{heinz2010,hayashikamigaito2025}, and state an open conjecture locating the construction in the mildly context-sensitive hierarchy.

Machine Learning.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.29111v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Predicting molecular magnetic properties often requires costly electronic-structure calculations that account for spin-orbit coupling. Inspired by the spinor nature of the underlying electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features alongside the integer-rank tensors used in conventional equivariant models. We initialize spinors from eigenvectors of an approximate Hamiltonian that includes spin-orbit coupling. The network preserves their rotation laws and makes predictions independent of arbitrary eigenbasis choices. Comparisons with geometry-only and Hamiltonian-informed baselines assess the benefit of this architecture beyond supplying electronic information. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves magnetic anisotropy predictions, including for unseen ligands. It also improves excitation-energy predictions for dysprosium candidates with unseen ligands, extending the benefit to rotationally invariant scalar targets. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, it predicts real electron-spin correlations and low-field nuclear relaxation rates more accurately despite static crystal-field errors similar to the Hamiltonian-informed baseline. This dynamical advantage extends from water to methanol without retraining. These results support spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism in the tested systems and show why model selection should be guided by accuracy on the intended physical observables.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted to NeurIPS SIMBIOCHEM II Workshop

Machine Learning.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.29196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Grounded and Faithful Vision-Language Models for Real-World Deployment (VLM4RWD). 16 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL

Machine Learning.title: Reconstruction differences rival individual differences in the fly compass connectome and break trained circuit models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.29205v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural network models are increasingly constructed from synapse-resolution connectomes, and the same circuit is now available in reconstructions from other animals and pipelines. We do not know whether such models are dependent on the reconstruction they are built from, and whether connectome differences are biological or measurement errors. We studied the Drosophila head-direction circuit in nine versions: four flies (male CNS, hemibrain, FlyWire, BANC) and five variants of the same fly varying only by thresholds, proofreading or synapse detection. Using wiring-based correspondences validated by anatomical labels, we place all differences on one scale. A change of synapse detection within one fly changed the circuit more than halfway to the smallest between-fly difference on four distance measures; proofreading differences were smaller but depended on the metric, and left and right halves of one fly differed no more than random halves. Networks trained on each wiring to hold a cued heading developed near-perfect ring attractors, but their error increased from below 1 degree to 10-28 degrees when all weights changed by 1%. Training on each wiring did not transfer to any other connectome, including other versions of the same fly; refitting thirty cell-type gains, we repaired filtering-level differences but remaining error depended on wiring distance. Training with noise lowered precision and gave only partial transfer. In imaging data, the fly compass drifted gradually in darkness. Connectome-constrained models should report the reconstruction they were built on and be tested for robustness across reconstructions.

Machine Learning.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.29680v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term.
  We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates.
  We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.

Machine Learning.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.30090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and unparseable. We present VX-One, a small multi-head network (100K--10M parameters) with calibrated typed outputs: a binary gate, a closed-set choice with an explicit unknown option where the benchmark supports it (and abstention elsewhere), and an ordinal score. Heads are temperature-calibrated, with 0.7--1.7 ms single-event CPU p50 latency. We evaluate UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP, and Kitsune baselines, and measure a Suricata-to-VX-One cascade over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Results are deliberately double-sided: on UNSW the gate ties the best baseline (0.9837+/-0.0002 versus MLP 0.9835+/-0.0013 across three seeds), while VX-One wins temporal CIC detection (0.734+/-0.022 versus 0.639+/-0.027) but loses multi-class attribution to XGBoost. Under leave-one-family-out, the gate detects all nine UNSW families but drops below chance on CIC recon; CIC trees transfer better. Suricata resolves only about 0.1% of attacks on flow reconstructions and 0.2--2.2% on payload-bearing PCAPs; the strictly by-day Phase 2 recovers only the in-scope DoS/DDoS share on the wave day (recall 0.34, precision 0.97). Calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partly survives. We contribute a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

Machine Learning.title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.31336v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

Machine Learning.title: Democratizing LLM Training with the Edge: Challenges, Systems, and the Road Ahead
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.32215v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.

Multimedia.title: AdShot: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Video Advertisement Clipping
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.33377v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.

Multimedia.title: MMFact: Simplifying Multimodal Misinformation Detection with Shared Resources and Tools
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.34162v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal misinformation detection methods often rely on different preprocessing pipelines and auxiliary resources, making experimental comparisons difficult to interpret. We present MMFact, a collection of shared resources and tools that simplifies this research workflow. It brings together 47 detector implementations and baselines, three multimodal datasets, and prepared materials ranging from semantic features to OCR, image descriptions, and external evidence. Compatible methods can use the same materials, reducing variation introduced by preprocessing and supporting fairer comparisons. A modular training and evaluation framework preserves method-specific designs while providing common experimental procedures. By treating prepared materials as a shared research resource, MMFact helps researchers focus on developing and evaluating detection methods.

Multimedia.title: Multimodal Concert Video Editing: System Design and Exploratory Evaluation
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.35816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Editing multi-camera concerts requires coordinated decisions about musical relevance, visual quality and cut timing. We present a modular framework that combines instrument activity from multitrack audio, visible instruments and image sharpness with beat-based timing and probabilistic camera selection. An interpretable scoring model links these components to the choice of views over complete shot intervals. Component tests and an exploratory expert study on a four-camera concert yield mixed assessments across the editing variants. The findings motivate extending local audiovisual relevance with contextual and sequence-level criteria. The architecture provides a basis for testing these extensions and studying how component behaviour affects the quality of complete edits.

Multimedia.title: The Paired Thermal Channel Is Two Orthogonal Axes: A Controlled Attribution Study of Calibration Cost and Detection Gain in Infrared Person Detection
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.33118v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The calibrated thermal channel in infrared person detection comprises two structurally orthogonal axes. True calibrated $\Delta T$ outperforms scale-matched grayscale pseudo-$\Delta T$ by $+0.0221$ mAP (paired Wilcoxon $p=0.0098$, Cohen's $d=+1.08$), confirming that the calibrated channel carries information the grayscale channel lacks. The calibration axis is driven by the joint pairing-scale condition. Preserving both paired correspondence and absolute calibrated scale raises expected calibration error (ECE) from $\approx 0.05$ to $0.142$. The $2\times 2$ interaction ($p=0.0059$) localizes the rise to this condition. Breaking either factor alone returns ECE to the broken-factor level (true-vs-const $p=0.002$; true-vs-shuffled $p=0.002$). Under post-hoc temperature scaling, the pairing cost survives recalibration ($p=0.002$), while the scale cost is largely absorbed ($p=0.16$). As regards the detection axis, the gain stems from structural de-structuring. Phase randomization, which destroys spatial structure while preserving per-sample variance, yields $+0.0185$ mAP over true $\Delta T$ on FLIR ADAS ($p=0.014$, $d=+0.96$). The FLAME~3 gain is $+0.0064$ mAP ($p=0.078$, n=8). On the calibration axis, the same intervention is insignificant on FLIR ADAS ($p=0.47$) but significant on FLAME~3 ($p=0.0078$). These findings rest on a five-arm controlled attribution with temperature-evidential learning (TEL) as the testbed. TEL obtains a single evidence-derived routing scalar together with a complementary diagnostic entropy, and establishes a finite-evidence degeneracy theorem proving that the acquisition product degenerates to this scalar with a closed-form bound. A physical $0.5^\circ$C threshold admits cross-dataset physical readings, whereas a gray threshold of $20$ inverts without physical interpretation.

Multimedia.title: IAR: An Interaction-Aware Approach to Post-Seek Recovery in Adaptive HLS Streaming
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.33120v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: After an unbuffered seek, an adaptive bitrate (ABR) player has little forward buffer at the new position, while its controller may retain a bandwidth estimate from earlier downloads. An expensive first request can delay resumption; later requests may interrupt playback while the buffer rebuilds. We introduce Interaction-Aware Recovery (IAR), a temporary layer around the hls.js ABR controller. After an unbuffered seek, IAR discounts the inherited estimate ({\gamma}=0.15) to set a representation ceiling. Normal adaptation continues below it until 8 s of forward buffer has been rebuilt. In a 200-run paired study spanning four network profiles, ten seek positions, and five strategies, a conservative first request reduced resume delay by a paired median of 2.008 s relative to standard hls.js. Keeping a low ceiling through recovery reduced later interruption under stronger degradation but lowered early presented bitrate. IAR and Fixed-Low-Recovery both used L0 in this campaign, so the results did not show an additional benefit from deriving the ceiling from inherited bandwidth. In 60 additional runs under a fixed Moderate profile, we reset the estimator to six controlled scalar priors. IAR's ceiling changed from L0 to L1 and L2 at the predicted thresholds. Resume and recovery times increased at those transitions; presented bitrate varied non-monotonically and was highest at L2. No stalls occurred. These reset-created priors do not reproduce complete, naturally evolved exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) histories. The results show the benefits and presented-quality costs of conservative post-seek recovery, without establishing an advantage for a history-derived ceiling over a fixed low ceiling.

Multimedia.title: Beyond Visible Speakers: Context-Aware Active Speaker Detection with Speaker Registration
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.33127v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.

Multimedia.title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.33413v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.

Multimedia.title: Freeze What Is Settled, Cache What Is Smooth: Spatial Freezing Keeps Step Caching in Its Low-Error Regime
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.34177v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers run tens of denoising steps. Training-free acceleration either reuses features across steps (step caching) or stops computing the regions an edit leaves untouched (region freezing), and the two have been combined before. We ask how a high speed-up target should be split between them. On Qwen-Image-2.1, freezing does more than remove tokens: it lowers the cost of every step, so the step cache can reach the same overall speed-up with a conservative threshold that keeps its error small. A per-step cost model fitted on development runs predicts held-out latency with a median error of 4.0% and reproduces the speed ceilings of the region methods we re-implemented (2.73$\times$ predicted vs. 2.70$\times$ measured for RegionE). Driving frozen tokens to the model's one-step $x_0$ estimate beats returning them to the reference image on every development sample, and in 90% of measured cases the composed error stays below the sum of the two individual errors. The resulting method, FreezePlan, keeps five full steps and gives the rest of the budget to TaylorSeer. On a pre-registered test split it runs 5.05$\times$ faster end to end at 29.8 dB PSNR to the original output, with no significant drop in a VLM judge score; TaylorSeer at 5.02$\times$ reaches 23.5 dB. The curve extends to 5.99$\times$ at 28.0 dB. Swapping in the region selectors of prior methods under our schedule lowers median PSNR by only 0.5--0.6 dB, which places the gain in the schedule and budget split rather than in the selector.

Multimedia.title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.34688v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.

Multimedia.title: ImageTTS: Repurposing Pretrained Image Diffusion Transformers for Speech Synthesis
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.34807v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Pretrained image-generation models have been successfully repurposed for various downstream visual tasks. Whether their learned representations and generative priors can transfer beyond vision to other modalities remains largely unresolved, particularly for speech synthesis, which requires linguistic fidelity and preservation of speaker identity from a short reference. We present ImageTTS, which repurposes FLUX.2 for speech synthesis by encoding pseudo-RGB log-mel spectrograms with its frozen image VAE and adapting only its pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) using conditional latent flow matching. This formulation disentangles two forms of vision-to-speech transfer: representation transfer through the image VAE and generative-prior transfer through DiT initialization. The frozen image VAE largely preserves intelligibility and speaker identity with 0.99 STOI and 0.95 speaker similarity, while image-pretrained DiT initialization accelerates convergence and improves linguistic accuracy, reducing WER from 4.2\% to 2.7\% at 100k matched updates relative to random initialization. The same framework supports both zero-shot and instruction-guided TTS and, when scaled to 100K hours of speech data, achieves 1.12\% WER on Seed-TTS test-en and a Style-ACC of 0.66 on CapSpeech, outperforming speech-native baselines trained on comparable data across both tasks. These results suggest that pretrained image models can transfer beyond architectural reuse, supplying useful latent representations and generative priors for intelligible and controllable speech synthesis.

Multimedia.title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.35757v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Visual search is ubiquitous in daily life, from locating keys in a messy apartment to finding a tool in a cluttered workshop or an application icon on a desktop screen. While visual attention is to a large extent driven by image content, research in psychology indicates that user cognitive states have a significant influence on attention allocation. A promising way to access information about cognitive states is via Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. Despite this potential, previous works in computational attention modeling have largely disregarded EEG, and related studies in psychology operate with abstract, simplistic stimuli, or even artificially guided search procedures. We bridge this gap with two contributions. First, we present EEGaze 140, the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of free visual search with realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye tracking recordings from 36 participants across 140 naturalistic scenes, covering two scenarios: searching for desktop icons and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. Second, we introduce EEGazeNet, the first method for human attention prediction in visual search that integrates EEG signals. Our approach consists of a EEG guided refinement stage that adapts the output of a state of the art saliency prediction method to the user current cognitive state. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze 140, we show that EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions.

Multimedia.title: Catalogue-Grounded Multimodal Attribution for Museum Video under Resource and Regulatory Constraints
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2603.11147v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Museum audiovisual archives are important records of visual culture, yet in-gallery video remains difficult to search because it lacks catalogue-compatible metadata. We propose CaGMulA, catalogue-grounded multimodal attribution for museum video: a locally deployable pipeline that combines video-language models, structured catalogue retrieval, and abstention-aware decision policies. The system summarises visible artworks, generates catalogue-style descriptions, and attributes title and artist only when evidence is sufficient. We evaluate VideoLLaMA2 and Qwen2-VL across four model configurations and four attribution modes on 18 in-gallery videos. Open-ended generation fails under conservative conditions, producing 0\% coverage across models. By contrast, closed-set catalogue retrieval reaches 100\% coverage with 62\% accepted title--artist correctness, while a verifier-gated hybrid mode reduces coverage to 50\% but improves accepted correctness to 78\%. The results show that reliable museum-video attribution is driven less by unrestricted generation than by catalogue grounding, visual retrieval, and selective abstention for curatorial review.

Multimedia.title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: Agentic Optimization for Image-to-Video Adherence
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2608.12290v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern black-box Image-to-Video (I2V) models offer powerful capabilities in automated content creation, yet their lack of fine-grained control and reliability presents significant challenges in professional workflows. Their inherent stochasticity causes minor variations in textual prompts or hyperparameters to yield drastically different outputs often necessitating inefficient, brute-force trial-and-error processes. To address these limitations, we introduce the ``Agentic Self-Improvement" framework, which reframes video synthesis into a closed-loop, goal-directed optimization. Our framework systematically navigates the generation parameter space using a novel two-stage approach. In the first stage, an iterative prompt optimization loop uses a multimodal Large Language Model (mLLM) to refine the input prompt. This refinement implements two automated evaluations: Davidsonian Scene Graph (DSG) queries ensure semantic adherence, and Common Mistake Questions (CMQ) for artifact detection. At the second stage, we use Bayesian optimization to efficiently co-optimize stochastic seeds and CFG scales. This search is guided by a suite of quality metrics, including the novel Video-Text Adherence (VTA) score derived from the DSG and CMQ evaluations. Our framework significantly outperforms unguided search methods: in human preference studies, videos generated via our agentic approach were strongly preferred over baseline outputs, achieving win rates up to 69\%. This work provides a practical and extensible methodology for enhancing the predictability and control of state-of-the-art video generation models, moving the field beyond speculative curiosities toward reliable, production-ready tools.

Multimedia.title: Steering the Flow: Inverting Face Recognition Models via Gradient-Guided Flow Matching
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2608.16791v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Model Inversion Attacks (MIAs) aim to reconstruct representative training samples of target identities from face recognition models, exposing critical security vulnerabilities. Existing methods typically rely on indirect guidance or highly stochastic guidance, making it difficult to stably optimize generation trajectories toward target facial images. In this paper, we propose Steering Flow Model Inversion (SFMI), a novel two-stage white-box model inversion method that reformulates inversion as a trajectory-steering task. Specifically, Step I, Learning a Generic Flow Matching Prior, pre-trains a generic unconditional Flow Matching model to encode the manifold of human faces as a robust prior. Step II, Attacking with Progressive Guidance Scheduler (PGS), injects time-dependent target-specific gradients during sampling. By backpropagating through the target model to obtain gradients from intermediate generated states, PGS progressively injects adaptive guidance signals into the vector field. This process effectively steers the current generative flow from random noise toward the high-density regions of the target class. Under an identity-disjoint cross-evaluation setting using the CelebA dataset, SFMI achieves an ACC of 0.9248, an FID of 22.61, and an LPIPS of 0.3874 on the ArcFace target. Extensive experiments on multiple target models demonstrate that SFMI achieves competitive state-of-the-art performance in attack success and visual fidelity under the evaluated white-box protocol.

Multimedia.title: Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention and Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion for Video Action Detection
Multimedia.summary:
arXiv:2610.29176v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In video action detection, modeling the temporal dependencies in continuous video streams is crucial. Previous methods based on deep neural networks can perform frame-level video recognition tasks. However, these methods struggle to model dynamic temporal patterns, facing challenges such as redundant frame information, difficulty balancing global and local features, and insufficient fusion of visual and textual features. To address these issues, we propose a video temporal attention module based on the Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention, which aggregates continuous temporal sequences into feature representations across diverse temporal scales while efficiently reducing redundancy. We also introduce a Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion module that leverages cross-attention at both latent and standard feature levels, achieving fine-grained fusion between video and textual features to enhance semantic alignment and feature interaction. Experimental results across multiple video recognition benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability.

Computation and Language.title: ReCoPII: A Relation-Grounded Framework for Building Contextual PII Masking Datasets
Computation and Language.summary:
arXiv:2610.35925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training contextual masking systems for personally identifiable information (PII) requires examples distinguishing maskable from preservable mentions of one entity type, but privacy restrictions limit access to real data. Author-based augmentation (SPY) labels mentions unrelated to the author as non-PII, presuming a single data subject and overlooking others. We propose ReCoPII (Relation-grounded Contextual PII masking), a framework that builds such data without this premise: it plans ontology-constrained entity relations, writes insertion sentences with placeholders, reconstructs annotations with code, checks the result with a separate LLM, and derives MASK/KEEP labels from entity relations. On Korean documents from six domains, it yields ReCoPII-Ko, a corpus with relation, privacy, and MASK/KEEP annotations, which we validate. Across 300 pairs, four annotators agree with 88.42% of its sampled KEEP labels, against 26.27% for SPY-style augmentation of the same sources.
